transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-09
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 54 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Security PM); Lisa Morgan (Veridian CISO), Tomás Ruiz (Head of Infra), Aisha Khan (Compliance), Ben Riley (DevOps), Sophie Leung (Legal)

Summary: quick SOC2/ISO posture walkthrough focused on evidence access, controls mapping, RBAC/SSO alignment, audit logging retention, data residency constraints for EU trials, and KMS/encryption integration. Agreed next steps around delivering reports and a KMS deep-dive.

Referenced artifacts:
- Redwood Trust Center (sample): https://redwood.example.com/trust-center (placeholder)
- Controls mapping template (Google Sheet): https://docs.google.com/example-controls-mapping (placeholder)
- SOC 2 Type II sample index & evidence manifest (to be shared)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, appreciate you making time. Quick roll call then we'll jump in.
[00:08] Lisa Morgan: Hi Maya, Lisa here. We've got Tomás, Aisha, Ben and Sophie on our side. Thanks.
[00:13] Diego Alvarez: Diego from Redwood, hi all.
[00:15] Priya Nair: Priya, security PM.
[00:18] Tomás Ruiz: Tomás, hi.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Cool. Purpose of the call is to walk through our SOC 2/ISO posture and show how you'd consume our reports and map controls, and then dig into KMS/encryption questions for your regulated workloads.
[00:32] Lisa Morgan: Yes, mostly evidence collection and whether Redwood can meet our ISO 27001 annex A mappings and the data residency controls for EU trials. Our legal also wants to understand key management options.
[00:45] Maya Chen: Great. Diego, want to start with a short overview of how we store audit logs and the KMS architecture?
[00:51] Diego Alvarez: Sure. So high-level, logs are retained in an immutable store, indexed, with retention policy per customer tier. For Hosted customers we provide 365-day retention by default, and Dedicated/Private can be configured longer. Logs are accessible via the console and can be exported into your SIEM via our connector. There are, uh, two layers of encryption at rest: platform disk encryption plus envelope encryption with a per-tenant data key. For KMS we support either Redwood-managed keys or customer-managed keys via AWS KMS, GCP KMS, or an HSM-backed solution in Private deployments.
[01:30] Aisha Khan: When you say envelope encryption, does that mean customer keys can be held in our KMS only?
[01:36] Diego Alvarez: Yes, for CMKs you can bring your own key—BYOK—and we only store a wrapped key. We support automatic key rotation and can also do external HSM integrations if you require FIPS 140-2 modules.
[01:46] Ben Riley: How are audit logs protected? If we need to demonstrate tamper-resistance during an audit, what's the chain?
[01:52] Diego Alvarez: Logs are write-once in the blob store with immutability flags; they're cryptographically signed at ingestion, and we keep an audit ledger that references the object hashes. For dedicated/private you'll also be able to route logs directly into your account or a customer-owned S3 bucket for full control.
[02:10] Lisa Morgan: Ok that helps. Sophie, any immediate legal asks?
[02:14] Sophie Leung: We need the SOC 2 Type II report and, importantly, the evidence manifest that ties controls to artifacts. Also we want to see the ISO 27001 scope statement and the Statement of Applicability if you have it.
[02:26] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll provide the Type II report and an evidence index. Priya will also surface the SoA and scope doc.
[02:33] Priya Nair: Yup I'll attach those to the share and mark sensitive fields. Note that some items in the evidence pack are redacted for customer privacy but we'll provide mapping references.
[02:41] Tomás Ruiz: On the controls mapping, we have our internal control IDs and we need a one-to-one mapping. How do you usually structure that?
[02:48] Maya Chen: We have a template that maps Redwood control IDs to common frameworks: SOC 2 CC, ISO Annex A, NIST CSF. We'll populate Redwood controls, the artifact filename, and then you can add your internal control IDs in a separate column. We'll share the sheet with edit rights.
[03:02] Aisha Khan: Can you also annotate which controls require on-prem or Private deployment for full compliance?
[03:07] Diego Alvarez: Absolutely—we'll flag controls that depend on Private deployment or dedicated infrastructure. For example host-level access controls are different in Hosted vs Private.
[03:15] [03:15] Lisa Morgan: Data residency — we need EU-only processing for certain datasets. How's regional routing handled?
[03:21] Diego Alvarez: Requests can be routed to EU regions based on policy, we can pin models to region, and for PII we support tenant-level residency where data and keys remain in the selected region. For hosted EU region we ensure data at rest and transit within EU; for additional guarantees we recommend Private or Dedicated with VPC-based networking.
[03:40] Tomás Ruiz: What's the failover behavior if a region is down — is data routed out?
[03:45] Diego Alvarez: By default we fail within the same geo; cross-region failover is opt-in and documented. For strict residency you can opt-out of cross-region fallback to ensure no egress.
[03:55] [04:00] Maya Chen: Quick pause — Lisa, do you have specific auditors or standards with custom requirements?
[04:05] Lisa Morgan: We use an external auditor for ISO and have internal SOC reviewers. They sometimes ask for raw evidence like config snapshots and user access lists.
[04:13] Priya Nair: We can provide time-bounded config exports and an admin activity log. We do redact customer identifiers where needed but will provide hashes and pointers for auditors.
[04:22] Aisha Khan: We will also need SSO/SAML metadata and RBAC role mappings — show us how Admin vs Operator roles map to your console permissions.
[04:31] Diego Alvarez: There's a role matrix we can export; we support SAML 2.0/Okta/Azure AD with SCIM provisioning. Role-based access aligns to resource-level permissions and we can provide a CSV mapping for your review.
[04:45] Ben Riley: Is there support for time-limited access for auditors, like temporary elevated roles or just share logs?
[04:51] Priya Nair: We support ephemeral access tokens for audit sessions and also pre-configured read-only auditor roles. For dedicated customers you can define short-lived bastion credentials.
[05:02] [05:20] Lisa Morgan: Ok, moving into KMS specifics — we have a Pharma crypto team that requires HSM-backed keys and key rotation proof. What's your evidence for rotation and key custody?
[05:30] Diego Alvarez: Rotation events are logged and the KMS audit trail includes who rotated which key, timestamps, and the rotation policy. If you're using your CMK, rotation is controlled by your KMS and the logs originate in your KMS; Redwood will record the wrapped-key changes and the binding event. For HSMs we can provide attestation materials subject to NDA.
[05:50] Lisa Morgan: Attestation would be necessary, yes.
[05:53] Sophie Leung: Also need to confirm data classification handling — how do you tag and segregate trial data vs public/non-sensitive tokens?
[06:01] Diego Alvarez: We support dataset-level labels; customers can tag content or route requests to model variants with stricter handling. We also have prefix caching rules to avoid cross-tenant leakage.
[06:14] Maya Chen: On the caching note, we have per-tenant cache isolation and an option to disable persistent prefix caching for sensitive datasets — that eliminates stored prompts on the platform.
[06:24] Tomás Ruiz: Good. What's the default retention for embeddings and prompt logs?
[06:28] Diego Alvarez: By default embeddings and prompt logs retained 90 days; configurable for Dedicated/Private. For strict compliance you can set to 0 days or route logs to your storage.
[06:38] [06:45] Aisha Khan: About SSO: we need SCIM provisioning and attribute mappings (email, jobTitle, department). Any gotchas?
[06:52] Priya Nair: We support SCIM and flexible attribute mapping. The common issue is duplicate accounts due to email normalization; we include guidance in the integration doc. We'll do a test sync in the KMS deep dive.
[07:02] Lisa Morgan: For ISO specifically, do you have a Statement of Applicability and the Annex A control mapping?
[07:08] Maya Chen: Yes, we maintain a SoA and can export Annex A mappings against our controls. We'll share that in the evidence bundle.
[07:15] Ben Riley: Are there any open control gaps we should be aware of?
[07:18] Priya Nair: There are a few roadmap items like longer-term retention analytics and some new tracer integrations; we document them in the SoA as 'planned' with expected timelines. None are high-risk for your use-case, but we'll call them out.
[07:33] [07:40] Sophie Leung: On legal/internals: need to confirm breach notification SLAs and data processing addendum terms.
[07:47] Maya Chen: Standard DPA is available, we can share the current template. Breach notification is 72 hours for incidents that affect customer data, and we also have an incident response playbook.
[07:58] Aisha Khan: Do you provide retained evidence for change control (patches, configuration changes)?
[08:05] Diego Alvarez: Yes, change control logs, CI/CD pipeline run artifacts, and deployment approvals can be exported. For Private deployments you can also supply pipeline run logs as part of the evidence.
[08:20] [08:30] Lisa Morgan: Let's walk through a sample control mapping scenario — for ISO A.9 (access control), what artifacts would map?
[08:38] Priya Nair: For A.9 we'd include the role matrix, SAML metadata, access reviews (quarterly), and privileged access logs. We'll annotate which are console artifacts vs environment-level artifacts.
[08:48] Tomás Ruiz: Do you perform periodic access reviews or is that on the customer?
[08:52] Priya Nair: We do platform-side access reviews for our staff; customers are responsible for reviewing their users. We can provide exported review logs for auditors.
[08:58] [09:05] Maya Chen: Quick question from Sophie: any contractual clauses around data subprocessing and subprocessors list?
[09:12] Priya Nair: We have a subprocessors list and an API to query current processors. We update customers before changes and include it in the Trust Center.
[09:20] Sophie Leung: Ok please include that list in the evidence.
[09:23] Maya Chen: Will do.
[09:25] [09:30] Ben Riley: On monitoring: what metrics/traces are available for SLA/latency evidence?
[09:36] Diego Alvarez: We provide per-route latency dashboards, token-level billing traces, and request/response traces for a configured retention window. For Dedicated customers we'll set longer retention and custom dashboards.
[09:49] Lisa Morgan: For our auditors, sometimes they ask for source-of-truth IP allowlist and ingress rules. Are those exportable?
[09:56] Diego Alvarez: Yes, network configs, security group rules, and IP allowlists can be exported and included in the evidence manifest. For Private deployments it's under your control.
[10:06] [10:15] Maya Chen: Great — we'll take a short pivot to talk KMS integration steps and then circle back to evidence timelines. Diego?
[10:21] Diego Alvarez: Steps: 1) Decide CMK vs Redwood-managed. 2) If CMK, exchange key ARN and set up key policy to allow Redwood to wrap/unwrap. 3) Configure envelope encryption in tenant settings. 4) Run integration test to verify wrapped-key exchange and rotation event logs. We'll provide a step-by-step runbook.
[10:40] Aisha Khan: For BYOK we require that Redwood never has unencrypted plaintext keys—only the wrapped key.
[10:45] Diego Alvarez: Correct, Redwood never stores plaintext CMKs. We store the wrapped key material and the encryption path uses your KMS for decryption during runtime.
[10:53] Tomás Ruiz: For Private, can we bring an HSM in our environment and have Redwood call it?
[10:58] Diego Alvarez: Yes, in Private deployments we can integrate with customer HSMs via a secure channel or run a sidecar that handles crypto operations.
[11:07] [11:20] Lisa Morgan: Are key usage logs retained in the KMS? We need rotation and usage history for audits.
[11:25] Diego Alvarez: Usage logs appear in your KMS audit trail; Redwood records binding events and references to the wrapped-key artifacts. We'll provide a combined ledger for auditors.
[11:36] Aisha Khan: Do you offer tokenization for dataset-level PII?
[11:40] Diego Alvarez: Not as a managed tokenization product today; we recommend pseudonymization and dataset isolation. Roadmap includes tokenization as a feature.
[11:49] [12:00] Maya Chen: Back to evidence — timeline expectations: we'll get the SOC 2 Type II and SoA out by Friday, the controls mapping template today, and the KMS architecture note next week. Does that align?
[12:10] Lisa Morgan: Yes that works. We'll aim to return the controls mapping with our control IDs in a week.
[12:16] [12:20] Sophie Leung: A quick legal note: we'll probably want the SOC 2 under NDA. Can you deliver via an encrypted share to our legal inbox?
[12:26] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll deliver via encrypted link and can add access controls.
[12:30] Ben Riley: On threat detection — do you surface anomaly detections for unusual API patterns?
[12:36] Diego Alvarez: We have built-in anomaly detection for request spikes and unusual usage patterns; alerts can be forwarded to your PagerDuty or webhook.
[12:45] [12:55] Tomás Ruiz: One more infra question: can we run periodic in-place security scans of the runtime?
[13:01] Priya Nair: We run third-party pentests and internal scans; for dedicated/private we can coordinate customer-led scans under a signed scope and time window.
[13:11] Lisa Morgan: Good to know.
[13:14] [13:20] Maya Chen: Ok let's open the floor for any final questions before we wrap.
[13:24] Aisha Khan: What about key compromise scenarios — how fast can you revoke access and rotate?
[13:30] Diego Alvarez: If you control the CMK you can revoke immediately via KMS; Redwood will handle re-wrapping and can replay requests to re-encrypt past persisted data if needed. For Redwood-managed keys, rotation and revocation happen with announced windows; for emergencies we have an incident process.
[13:48] Sophie Leung: We'll want the incident playbook as part of the evidence.
[13:52] Priya Nair: We'll include the incident response playbook in the bundle.
[13:57] [14:05] Maya Chen: A quick recap of commitments: send SOC2 Type II and SoA by 2025-07-11, controls mapping template today, KMS note by 2025-07-18, and schedule a KMS deep-dive for week of 2025-07-21.
[14:20] Lisa Morgan: Sounds good. Thank you all.
[14:22] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with calendar invites and the share links.
[14:28] (end of recording)

Notes on transcription quality: automatic transcription with occasional mis-heard technical terms (e.g., some Kubernetes/VPC mentions might be off). Use the attached artifacts for canonical names and docs.
